tts.m16.l1:
Why it matters: traders do not trade the printed number in isolation; they trade how it compares with what was already priced. Knowing who publishes a series, what it measures, and when it is released (including the publisher's time zone) is part of reading it.

Decision exercise (fictional paper): two inflation prints land the same week. Series A is a headline CPI figure from a national statistics agency. Series B is a trimmed-mean or core measure from the same agency. Write which one your paper rate-sensitive position should treat as more relevant and why, then check the agency's own description rather than a social-media summary.

Limitations and common errors: series are revised; seasonal adjustment methods change; and one month is not a trend. Do not treat a PMI from one provider as if every PMI used the same construction. S&P Global's 50.0 no-change wording applies to its PMIs; other providers publish their own methodologies. Timestamps without a time zone invite look-ahead mistakes when you combine US, European and Australian releases.
tts.m16.l2:
Why it matters: a strong print that matches consensus can be a non-event, while a small miss can reprice an entire rate path.

Worked decision (fictional): consensus unemployment is 4.1% and the print is 4.1%, but wage growth prints 0.4 percentage points above consensus. Bond yields rise. The labour-market headline was not the surprise; the wage component was. Journal the surprise, not only the level.

Common errors: confusing a forecast beat with a profitable trade; ignoring what rate futures already implied; and treating after-the-fact narratives as if they were your pre-trade thesis. If you cannot state the consensus and the implied move before the release, you are not prepared to trade the event.
tts.m16.l3:
Why it matters: company-level catalysts can dwarf a well-reasoned valuation view in a single session. Sizing before a binary event is a risk decision, not an afterthought.

Decision exercise: pick one listed company and build a one-week catalyst calendar from primary sources only (exchange announcements, official regulator or court lists, published earnings dates). Mark any item you found only on social media as unverified. Decide in advance whether your paper position will be cut, held, or avoided.

Limitations: continuous-disclosure rules and insider-trading laws differ by jurisdiction. The ASX and ASIC wording in this module is general education about Australia, not legal advice and not a statement of penalties. When in doubt, do not trade on information that may not be public.
tts.m16.l4:
Why it matters: bad information is an execution and ethics risk, not just an inconvenience.

A practical verification sequence: (1) identify the original publisher; (2) open that publisher's page or filing, not a screenshot; (3) note the time zone and whether the item is new; (4) ask what would falsify it; (5) if you cannot complete those steps, the default is no new paper trade.

Common errors: forwarding an AI summary that invented a source; treating a blog recap as a filing; and ignoring that some news is recycled commentary on an announcement from days earlier.
tts.m16.l5:
Why it matters: event risk is where otherwise careful sizing gets abandoned just this once.

Decision exercise: write a one-line rule that states when you will not open a new paper position (for example, implied event move more than twice the recent daily range, or an unverified headline). Then apply it to next week's calendar. Strategic no-trading is a valid output of a risk process.

Common errors: adding size into an event to make back an earlier loss; holding a leveraged product into a binary print against plan; and changing the rule after you see the number.
tts.m16.l6:
Timezone and session addendum: a US CPI release at 08:30 Eastern Time is already afternoon or evening in Australia. If your data stamp is stored as a naive local time, a backtest can accidentally treat that print as known during the Australian cash session. Always store event times with an explicit time zone and convert before deciding whether information was available.

The playbook's purpose is process evidence: you can show you listed the event, sized in advance, and journaled any breach. It is not a claim that following a calendar makes event trading profitable.
tts.m17.l1:
Why it matters: a moving average is only a description of past prices. It becomes a trading rule only when you specify entry, exit, size and costs.

Decision exercise: write close greater than the 200-day simple moving average as a complete rule, including whether you trade the close or the next open. If you cannot state the fill, you do not yet have a testable idea.

Limitations: the 200-day choice is a convention, not a law. In strong trends it can keep you in; in ranges it can whipsaw. Never treat a single moving-average cross as proof of an edge.
tts.m17.l2:
Why it matters: mean-reversion tools describe how extended a price is versus a recent window. They do not know whether the window is still the relevant regime.

Worked check: z = (46 - 50) / 2 = -2.0 says the price is two standard deviations below a 20-day mean. That can be a fading candidate in a range or the first day of a decline. The tool cannot tell you which.

Common errors: buying every oversold print; changing the lookback after a loss so that the last signal would have been skipped; and forgetting that a z-score uses the same prices that already moved against you.
tts.m17.l3:
Why annualisation needs a stated convention: multiplying a daily standard deviation by the square root of 252 is a common method for exchange-traded assets that rest on weekends. Using 365 is a common choice for assets that price every calendar day, such as many crypto markets. Both assume returns are independent enough that variance adds linearly with time. If returns are serially correlated, that square-root rule misstates horizon risk. Always write the factor you used (252, 365, 12 for monthly, or another) and do not mix frequencies inside one statistic.

Decision exercise: a daily standard deviation of 1.0% annualises to about 15.9% with sqrt(252) and about 19.1% with sqrt(365). The gap is a convention choice, not extra skill.
tts.m17.l4:
Why it matters: two people can look at the same chart and draw different support lines. That subjectivity is why patterns must be turned into rules before they can be tested.

Decision exercise: pick one pattern you like and write entry, invalidation and exit without pointing at a picture. If you need the picture to define the rule, it is not yet testable.

Common errors: drawing the line after the bounce; ignoring that many others see the same round number; and treating a pattern name as evidence.
tts.m17.l5:
Why it matters: an untested chart story cannot be distinguished from hindsight.

Minimum test package before you trust a paper rule: exact definition, more than one market or period, costs and delays, trade count, and a comparison with a naive benchmark such as buy-and-hold or random entries with the same exits. Module 20 then asks whether the test itself was honest.
tts.m17.l6: Link to data quality: the exact rule above still fails if the price series is wrong. A split-unadjusted series can create a false breakdown. A timezone-naive series can create a false close-already-known-at-the-open signal. Test the rule on a series you can explain, including how corporate actions and missing bars were handled. The school's synthetic mini-backtest (datasets/synthetic_mini_backtest.csv) is a practice file for those checks, not a source of market edge.
tts.m18.l1:
Why it matters: most large trading failures begin with a position that was too large for the stop distance, not with a wrong opinion about direction.

The formula shares = (account x risk %) / (entry - stop) assumes you actually will exit near that stop. If the market can gap, the realised loss can exceed the planned R. Size is therefore a plan, not a guarantee.

Decision exercise (fictional): account A$80,000, risk 0.75%, entry A$12.40, stop A$11.80. Planned risk = A$600. Stop distance = A$0.60. Size = 1,000 shares, notional A$12,400. Write whether a 3x gap through the stop would still be acceptable under your heat rule. If not, cut size or skip the trade.

Common errors: using account percentage of notional instead of account percentage of risk; placing the stop after you see the fill; and rounding size up to make it worth it.
tts.m18.l2:
Why it matters: a fixed share count in a quiet week becomes an oversized bet when volatility doubles.

Worked case: risk A$400, ATR A$1.00, stop at 2 x ATR = A$2.00, size = 200 shares. If ATR rises to A$2.00, the same rule produces 100 shares. That is the point of volatility sizing: it translates a money risk cap into fewer shares when the market is moving more.

Limitation: ATR is backward-looking. It will not warn you the day before a gap. Treat it as an adapter, not a forecast.
tts.m18.l3:
Why it matters: correlation is how diversification succeeds or fails. It is not stable.

Correlation-regime case (fictional numbers, for process practice, not a historical index claim): in a calm window four bank shares show pairwise correlations around 0.55. You treat four 0.50% risk slots as separate and record 2.0% heat. In a stress week the same pairs print realized correlations around 0.90. The four slots now behave much more like one concentrated 2% bet. The heat number did not change; the independence assumption did.

Decision exercise: group your current paper positions by a shared driver (same sector, same commodity, same currency, same rates view). Cap each group, not only the sum of stops. When you cannot estimate correlation honestly, assume it is high.

Limitations: a single correlation number is an average of a window. It can be low right up until the window that hurts you. No correlation estimate guarantees that diversification will work in the next crisis.
tts.m18.l4:
Why it matters: a stop is an instruction about ordinary paths. Gaps, halted trading and thin books can send the fill far beyond the instruction.

Gap and liquidity stress (fictional): 500 shares, entry A$20.00, stop A$19.20, planned risk A$400. An overnight announcement opens the share at A$17.60 on a wide A$17.40/A$17.90 quote with little depth. A stop-market order can fill near A$17.60 or worse if it walks a thin book: realised loss about A$1,200, or 3R, before brokerage. If you needed that exit during a trading halt, you may not be able to trade at all until the auction, which can be further away.

Decision exercise: before any overnight or event-held paper position, write a gap multiple you are willing to accept (for example 3x the planned stop distance) and the resulting stressed loss. If that stressed loss breaches your per-trade or group cap, reduce size or do not hold through the event.

Common errors: believing a stop caps the loss at exactly 1R; using marketable orders that are large relative to displayed depth; and treating paper fills at the stop price as realistic for live gaps. Nothing in this module guarantees a maximum drawdown.
tts.m18.l5:
Why it matters: drawdown ladders and heat caps are pre-commitments you make while calm so that you do not negotiate with yourself while losing.

They are not forecasts and they are not guarantees. A 10% pause rule does not mean the account cannot fall more than 10%: correlated gaps, skipped stops and added risk can all drive a deeper path. State that clearly in any paper risk policy.

Value at risk and expected shortfall (definitions). The Basel Committee's market-risk terminology (Minimum capital requirements for market risk, January 2019 rev. February 2019, MAR10.17-10.18) describes value at risk (VaR) as a measure of the worst expected loss on a portfolio of instruments resulting from market movements over a given time horizon and a pre-defined confidence level, and expected shortfall (ES) as a measure of the average of all potential losses exceeding the VaR at that confidence level. Those are regulatory-terminology definitions for bank market risk, used here as clear public wording. They are not a claim that a retail paper account must run a bank internal model, and they are not a maximum-loss promise.

Worked historical-style illustration (fictional sample, not market data): suppose 100 equally likely daily P&L outcomes, and the five worst losses are 2.4%, 1.9%, 1.6%, 1.4% and 1.3% of equity. A common teaching reading of one-day 95% historical VaR is the fifth-percentile loss, 1.3% of equity (A$1,300 on A$100,000). An inclusive average of those five tail losses, a teaching stand-in for expected shortfall at the same cutoff, is (2.4 + 1.9 + 1.6 + 1.4 + 1.3) / 5 = 1.72% (A$1,720). Basel's wording says ES averages losses exceeding VaR; some implementations average the tail at or beyond the cutoff. State which sample rule you used. Either way, ES is larger than VaR because it describes how bad the tail is, not only where the tail begins.

Limitations you must be able to recite: VaR does not say how large losses beyond the cutoff can be; a 95% VaR of A$1,300 does not cap the loss at A$1,300. Historical VaR assumes the sample window represents the future and can miss a new crisis. Parametric VaR that assumes a thin-tailed distribution can understate crash risk. Neither VaR nor ES is a drawdown figure: drawdown is a multi-day path. Neither includes the extra loss from exiting a larger size than the market can absorb (liquidity horizon, MAR10.20, is the time assumed to be required to exit or hedge without materially affecting prices in stressed conditions). A calm-window VaR that used low correlations will be too small if correlations rise. No risk statistic, stop, or ladder guarantees the next drawdown.
tts.m18.l6:
Crisis and correlation addendum (process case, fictional): imagine your paper book holds three iron-ore producers and two Australian banks into a risk-off week. Individual stops still sum to 2.5% heat, under a 3% cap. On the stress Monday all five gap down together as the shared drivers (China demand news and a jump in funding costs) move at once. Pairwise realized correlations jump, liquidity thins, and two of the stops fill beyond the planned price. Stressed loss is larger than both headline heat and any calm-window VaR you had scribbled from the previous month.

What the case is for: practising group caps, gap multiples, and the decision to trade or not trade. What it is not: a prediction of any named historical crash, a template that the next crisis will match, or a promise that following the ladder would have kept the loss inside a published number.

If a calculation or an uploaded AI recommendation says you may exceed the heat cap because VaR looks fine, decline it. Risk limits outrank a single statistic.
tts.m19.l1:
Why it matters: R converts every trade into the same risk units so that a A$200 win on a A$100 risk and a A$2,000 win on a A$1,000 risk are both +2R. Without that, you cannot compare process quality across different sizes.

Decision exercise: from your last five paper trades, compute each R-multiple using the planned stop distance, not the realised gap, if you want the process view, and also record the realised multiple if a gap occurred. Expectancy uses whatever definition you pre-commit to; changing it after the fact is a reporting error.

Limitation: expectancy is an average. A positive average with a few huge winners can hide a strategy that usually loses.
tts.m19.l2:
Why it matters: marketing for trading services often leads with win rate because it sounds like skill. The arithmetic does not care.

Worked reminder: 80% winners of 0.2R and 20% losers of 1.2R gives 0.16 - 0.24 = -0.08R. High accuracy, negative expectancy. Always pair win rate with payoff and with costs.
tts.m19.l3:
Sharpe annualisation, stated carefully. If you compute a Sharpe ratio from daily excess returns with mean mu_d and standard deviation sigma_d, a common annualisation is (mu_d / sigma_d) times sqrt(N), where N is 252 for many exchange-traded series or another stated factor. Equivalently, annualise the mean by multiplying by N and the standard deviation by sqrt(N), then divide. Sharpe's 1994 article warns that such annualising assumes no serial correlation; if returns are autocorrelated, the annualised figure is distorted. Do not annualise a two-week sample and present it as a comparable yearly Sharpe. State the risk-free or benchmark series, the return frequency, and N.

Sortino replaces total volatility with downside deviation, so two strategies with the same Sharpe can have different Sortino ratios if one has more upside volatility. Neither ratio is a promise of future returns, and both can look attractive on short, lucky samples.

Decision exercise: using fictional monthly excess returns with mean 0.8% and standard deviation 2.0%, a monthly Sharpe is 0.40. Multiplying by sqrt(12) gives about 1.39 only if you accept the independence assumption. Write that assumption next to the number.
tts.m19.l4:
Why it matters: without a standard error you cannot tell a real-looking average from noise.

A confidence interval that includes zero means you have not established a positive edge, even if the point estimate is positive. That is a reason for patience or for more data, not a reason to increase size. Regime change can make even a large historical sample misleading.
tts.m19.l5:
Why it matters: the easiest way to invent skill is to hide trades, costs, or losing periods.

An honest paper statement labels itself paper, states the content version of any rules, and separates human-discretion results from AI-assisted or uploaded-strategy results. Mixing those tracks is a reporting error.
tts.m19.l6:
Verification of the nine-loss-streak remark (added so the figure is not unexplained precision). Assumptions: 120 independent trades, each a loss with probability 0.58 (the complementary 42% win rate used in this fictional report), and a streak meaning nine losses in a row anywhere in the sequence. Under those assumptions an exact recurrence (a short Markov chain that tracks the current loss run and absorbs at nine) gives probability 0.3053 of at least one nine-loss run. A Monte Carlo of 200,000 independent sequences with seed 20261107 produced 0.3051. The earlier wording about a 30% chance matches this calculation; it is not a market forecast and it is not valid if trades are dependent or the loss rate is different. A naive count of 112 overlapping windows times 0.58 to the ninth overstates the probability (about 0.83) because the windows are not independent.

The broader lesson stands: painful streaks are compatible with a modest positive expectancy. They are not, by themselves, proof that the edge died, and they are not proof that you should double size to recover.

VaR versus drawdown: the fictional 11R max drawdown is a path statistic. It can exceed any single-period VaR you compute on daily R. Do not quote VaR as if it capped that path.
tts.m20.l1:
Why it matters: a beautiful backtest can be a bookkeeping error.

Data-quality session (core ideas you must be able to apply):

Timezone and session. A bar labelled 10:00 without a zone cannot be compared across Sydney, London and New York. If you use a US close to decide an Australian opening trade on the same calendar date, you may be using a price that has not yet happened in Sydney. Store timestamps with a time zone.

Corporate actions. A 2-for-1 split halves the raw price overnight. On unadjusted data that looks like a 50% crash and can trigger every breakdown rule you have. Use a split-adjusted series for return calculations and keep a separate corporate-action log so you can audit the adjustment. Dividends create a similar gap on price-return series; total-return series include them.

Fees and financing. Mid-to-mid backtests omit spread, brokerage, borrow and overnight financing. If the apparent edge is smaller than a conservative cost assumption, it is not an edge you have shown.

Delisting and survivorship. A universe of today's index members drops companies that failed, were acquired, or were removed earlier. Those missing names are often the losing trades. A survivorship-free study includes them up to the delist or removal date.

Missing data, stale prints and halts. Carrying the last price forward through a halt or a missing session invents zero-change returns and can create false signals. A tradable_flag of zero means do not treat this print as an executable price.

Lag versus look-ahead. Information must be available at the decision time. Using a bar's close to trade that same bar's open is look-ahead unless your written rule and fill model both say you trade the close. Future columns such as next_day_return must never be inputs to a signal.

The school's file datasets/synthetic_mini_backtest.csv is a SYNTHETIC practice series (seed 20261107, Australia/Sydney dates, no market data and no order book) built so you can see a raw split, a halt, a missing session, honest lagged signals, look-ahead signals, costs, and an in-sample versus out-of-sample split. It is not historical evidence of alpha.
tts.m20.l2:
Why it matters: if you look at the holdout while you develop, it is no longer a holdout.

Decision exercise: write the date you freeze development before you compute any out-of-sample number. If you then change a parameter, the holdout is contaminated and you must say so.

Walk-forward is not a magic fix: if each window secretly peeks, stitching the windows still peeks.
tts.m20.l3:
Why it matters: trying many ideas and reporting the winner is a selection process, even if each idea looked reasonable.

Keep a research log of how many variants you tried, including the ones you discarded. Without that count you cannot interpret a significant result. Bonferroni is a simple, conservative adjustment, not the only possible one, and it does not repair a contaminated holdout.
tts.m20.l4:
Why it matters: an edge that exists only at mid prices, or only against no benchmark, is usually not an edge.

Decision exercise: re-run one paper rule with doubled costs and with a one-bar delay. If the result collapses, write cost- or delay-fragile rather than promising.
tts.m20.l5:
Why it matters: credibility is a checklist, not a feeling after a good month.

Even a fully checked paper result is not evidence that you will be competent or profitable with real money. Live trading adds latency, partial fills, emotions and operational errors that a simulation does not contain.
tts.m20.l6:
Worked mini-backtest (SYNTHETIC file, not a market study). Using datasets/compute_backtest.py with seed 20261107:

The generated raw series includes a 2-for-1 split. The unadjusted close-to-close return on that day is about -50.7%; the split-adjusted return is about -1.3%. That gap is exactly the corporate-action trap: a rule on raw prices can read a split as a crash.

A halt day and a missing day are flagged tradable_flag = 0. Using those rows as ordinary closes would invent a tradable print.

A long-only rule (hold when the lagged split-adjusted close is above an N-day average, fill the next open) is run for N in {5, 10, 15, 20, 30} on the first 120 rows (in-sample) with 10 basis points of cost each way. The best in-sample honest net result in this invented path is N = 15 at about +0.75%. The same N on the unused last 60 rows is about -3.97% net. Choosing N by the in-sample ranking and quoting only +0.75% would have been overfitting.

On that same in-sample window, the invalid look-ahead version (decide and fill on the same close) prints about +2.03% net for N = 15, larger than the honest figure. The extra is an artefact of using information that was not available at the open.

None of these percentages is a forecast, a claim of alpha, or a reason to trade the rule. They exist so you can re-run the script and obtain the same numbers. If your own rerun differs, you are not looking at this file or this seed.

Common additional errors: putting next-period returns into the signal file; downloading a survivorship-biased constituent list and calling it a universe; and presenting polished statistics after you already peeked. This course does not compute a deflated Sharpe statistic in this version; if you see one elsewhere, treat it as another adjustment that still cannot prove future profits.
tts.m21.l1:
Why it matters: a plan you have not written will not be the plan you follow after a loss.

Process, not outcome, is the grading target. A losing trade that obeyed the plan scores better than a winning trade that broke a risk rule. That is uncomfortable, and it is the point.

Human learning and AI-strategy learning are separate tracks. Completing lessons and paper journals in this school does not automatically approve an uploaded strategy, and a paper-tested uploaded strategy does not complete the school on your behalf. Keep the records apart so that neither track borrows credibility from the other.
tts.m21.l2:
Why it matters: most broken risk rules are broken for emotional reasons that feel rational in the moment. A structured process exists to pre-commit while you are calm.

A practical psychology loop:

1. Before the session, precommitment. Write the markets you may trade, the maximum number of new paper trades, the per-trade risk, the heat cap, and the conditions that force no trading (drawdown ladder, unverified news, upcoming binary event outside the plan, or an emotional state you have named in advance such as anger after a loss).

2. During the session, a short checklist before each order: Is this a planned setup? Is the size calculated from the stop? Is the correlated group still inside its cap? Am I opening this to recover a loss? If any answer fails, the trade is a no.

3. Losing streaks are mathematically ordinary. Module 19 showed that a nine-loss run can occur about 30% of the time in a 120-trade sample with a 58% loss rate under independent-trade assumptions. A streak is information to review, not an automatic verdict that you should abandon the plan or double size.

4. Revenge is the urge to place a new trade quickly so that the loss does not count. Cooling-off rules (for example no new trade after three losses in a day, or after any critical-mistake flag) are precommitments against that urge.

5. Overconfidence is the mirror image after a winning streak: widening size because I am seeing it clearly now. Size stays at the precommitted fraction until you change the written plan in a review, not mid-session.

6. Strategic no-trading is a successful output. When a gate fails, the correct action is to stand aside. No-trade days are not laziness in this framework; they are rule-following. Journal them as such.

7. After the session, separate process marks from P&L. Ask what you would repeat if the outcome had been the opposite.

This loop does not make anyone an excellent trader and does not remove emotion. It makes emotion visible and reviewable.
tts.m21.l3:
Why it matters: skill without integrity is still harm, and in markets it can also be unlawful. This module gives general education, not legal advice and not a schedule of penalties, which vary by jurisdiction and change.

Honesty includes how you talk about paper results. Presenting simulated marks as live performance, or as proof you are a qualified trader, is a reporting failure even if no law is cited here.
tts.m21.l4:
Why it matters: fluent language is not the same as a checked fact or a safe order.

Upload Skills (teaching an AI trader) should follow the same rails as any other strategy change: you upload or describe a method; the system (or a reviewer) restates what it understood; you correct misunderstandings; the method is paper-tested with costs; it receives a version number, results and an approval status; and it must not bypass written risk limits. An uploaded prompt that says ignore the stop, increase size to recover, or this cannot lose is rejected, not tested for profit. Approval is a process state, not a certificate of excellence.

Naive trust, pasting a prompt and enabling it because the wording sounds expert, is a critical process mistake. It is different from using AI to draft a journal entry or to check arithmetic, which you still verify.

Human-school progress and AI-strategy approval remain separate records. Do not let a high quiz score stand in for an untested upload, or a lucky uploaded backtest stand in for completed coursework.
tts.m21.l5:
Why it matters: finishing a course creates a tempting story about being ready for live risk. That story is not evidence.

What completion can mean: you demonstrated a paper process against a published rubric. What it cannot mean: industry accreditation, a licence, a prediction of profit, or proof that you will execute well with real money. Simulation, including this app's paper mode, cannot by itself evidence live-trading competence.

If you later consider real money, that is a personal financial decision outside this course. This school does not instruct you to go live and does not represent that any paper result will survive contact with live markets, taxes, product rules or your own behaviour.
tts.m21.l6:
Capstone scoring, stated as a product default rather than an owner-made law. The 80% quiz pass mark, the suggestion of at least 30 journaled paper trades, the 0-3 rubric, an average at least 2.0 with no criterion at 0, and critical-mistake remediation are configurable defaults proposed for the product. They are not a regulator's standard and not an automatic certification. Changing them is a server-side configuration decision, not something a learner or an AI upload can waive in order to pass.

Critical-mistake remediation (default behaviour): if the journal or practical shows a critical breach, oversize beyond the stated multiple of planned risk, heat or correlation-cap breach, trading through a halt rule, widening a stop after entry, no exit plan on a leveraged position, holding leverage into an unplanned expiry or binary event, or misreporting results, the module is marked remediation required even if the quiz passed. The learner submits a written mistake review and one corrected paper trade (or a documented no-trade decision if the right correction was not to trade). Until that is recorded, the capstone is not a pass.

Profit is not a pass criterion. A negative expectancy over the paper sample can still pass if process, risk arithmetic and honesty meet the rubric; a profitable sample can fail if a critical mistake is unremediated or if reporting is incomplete.

Human versus AI evidence: capstone journals are evidence about the human learner's process. Uploaded-strategy paper tests are evidence about that strategy version. Neither is live-competence evidence; neither is accreditation.

No drawdown number in the plan is a guarantee. The capstone asks whether you stress-tested gaps and correlation, not whether the future obeyed your stress number.
tts.m01.l1:
Why it matters: when something goes wrong, the failure sits in a specific part of this chain (broker routing, matching, clearing, settlement, or registry). Knowing who does what tells you whom to ask and which delay is normal.

Decision exercise: map one paper share trade from your intention to a settled owner of record. Name the broker, venue, clearer and registry in general terms. Then write one sentence on a cost or delay that could appear at each step.

Common errors: treating the last traded price as a promise of your fill; assuming the broker is the exchange; and forgetting that paper fills in this app never reach a real venue.
tts.m01.l2:
Why it matters: the spread is the first, most reliable trading cost. If you ignore it, every backtest is too optimistic.

Decision exercise: a quote is bid A$3.40 / ask A$3.48 with 400 shares on the offer. You need 2,000 shares immediately. Mid is A$3.44, but a market buy will walk beyond A$3.48 if deeper book is worse. Write whether you would use a limit, split the order, or skip the name.

Common errors: quoting spread in cents without converting to percent of price; looking only at the top of book; and treating a one-share top-of-book print as evidence the stock is liquid.
tts.m01.l3:
Why it matters: order type is how you express a trade-off between price certainty and execution certainty. There is no type that gives both in a stressed market.

Decision exercise: you are willing to own ABC only at A$10.00 or better, and you do not want a fill at A$10.30 if the market runs. That is a limit order, not a market order. If you instead need to exit a leveraged position immediately, a marketable order may be the lesser evil, but you must accept price uncertainty, including a gap through any stop.

Common errors: using stop-market orders in thin names as if they were guaranteed exits at the trigger; leaving GTC limits active into earnings; and confusing a stop-limit (which may never fill) with a stop-market (which may fill far away).
tts.m01.l4:
Why sessions and time zones belong in market mechanics, not only in later data-quality notes. The same calendar date is not the same information set in Sydney, London and New York. An Australian cash-market decision made at 10:15 Sydney time cannot honestly use a New York close from later that same date. Store timestamps with an explicit zone and convert before asking what was known.

Auctions concentrate orders and can print far from the prior close, especially after news or at the open after a gap. Settlement then determines when cash and title move. As this lesson already notes, ASX cash equities were T+2 as of 7 Nov 2026 with T+1 under consideration, and most US securities moved to T+1 from 28 May 2024. Always re-check the venue.

Decision exercise: pick one ASX name and one US name and write, for a Tuesday trade, the weekday on which settlement would occur under the cycles taught here, skipping a mid-week public holiday in one market as a thought experiment.

Common errors: treating session times as interchangeable; ignoring auctions; and spending unsettled sale proceeds as if they were cleared cash.
tts.m01.l5:
Why it matters: fragmentation means the price you see on one screen may not be the price you can hit in size.

Decision exercise: using the fictional A$29 round-trip cost on a A$5,000 position (0.58%), calculate how large a subsequent gain you need just to break even after a matching exit cost if you already paid the entry half. If the idea's expected edge is smaller than total round-trip cost, it is not a trade.

Common errors: comparing brokers only on headline commission; forgetting exchange or FX conversion fees on foreign names; and assuming paper mid-price fills will be available live.
tts.m01.l6:
Queue-position note: this course does not give you auction-imbalance data or a full queue model to practise on, and paper engines usually ignore time priority. You should still understand the idea: at a given price, earlier orders typically fill first, so joining a long queue at a popular limit can leave you unfilled while the price moves away. Measure that as opportunity cost, not as a hidden loss in P&L.

If displayed depth is smaller than your order, do not assume the next levels are as generous as the first. Size to what you can see or use a limit.
tts.m02.l1:
Why it matters: a share is a residual claim. That is why equity can go to zero after creditors are paid, and why dilution and splits change share count without automatically changing your economic percentage if you participate equally.

Decision exercise: you own 1% of a fictional company. It issues new shares equal to 25% of the existing count and you do not take up your rights. Your ownership becomes 1 / 1.25 = 0.8%. Write that outcome in one sentence before you discuss whether the issue price was attractive.

Common errors: treating a split as a gain or loss; ignoring that unpaid rights expire; and ranking ordinary shares above lenders in a failure.
tts.m02.l2:
Why it matters: an ETF is a package of rules, fees and counterparties, not a magic version of the index.

Decision exercise: two funds track similar exposures. Fund A is physically backed with a 0.10% MER. Fund B is synthetic with a lower MER. Using Moneysmart's warning that synthetic ETFs carry extra counterparty risk, write which extra question you would ask about Fund B before comparing fees.

Limitations: daily-reset leveraged and inverse ETFs are designed around a daily objective. Multi-day results can diverge from the headline multiple, as in the SEC's -10% then +10% example where the index ends about -1% and a 2x fund ends about -4%.
tts.m02.l3:
Why it matters: you cannot interpret an index move unless you know what the index is designed to represent.

This course does not claim a single weighting method for every well-known index. DJIA and Nikkei 225 are described by their providers as price-weighted (see the evidence register). Many other major indices use some form of float-adjusted capitalisation weighting, but you should read the current methodology for the index you study rather than infer it from a neighbour. Equal-weight and total-return versions answer different questions.

Decision exercise: if a high-priced member dominates a price-weighted basket, a split that halves that price (with a divisor adjustment) changes its influence. Explain in one sentence why the index provider adjusts the divisor.
tts.m02.l4:
Why it matters: concentration is a hidden active bet inside a passive basket.

Decision exercise: using the fictional 60/30/10 weights, estimate the index move if A falls 8% and B and C each rise 4%. Result: 0.60 x -8% + 0.30 x 4% + 0.10 x 4% = -4.8% + 1.2% + 0.4% = -3.2%. The large member still dominated.

Common error: calling a cap-weighted index diversified without checking top-10 weight.
tts.m02.l5:
Why it matters: the same company can trade as different instruments, in different currencies, during different hours.

Decision exercise: a depositary receipt rises 2% while the home-market share is unchanged and the home currency strengthened 2% against the receipt currency. Before calling that an arbitrage, convert both prices to one currency and check whether they represent the same claim and the same number of underlying shares.

Common errors: comparing unconverted prices; ignoring dual-class voting differences; and treating an after-hours print in one venue as the official close in another.
tts.m02.l6: Decision reminder: choose the instrument that matches the risk you intend to take. A broad ETF can still be concentrated. A five-stock basket reduces some single-name risk and adds others. A leveraged daily ETF adds path-dependence. Write the intended risk first, then pick the wrapper.
tts.m03.l1:
Why it matters: price return and total return answer different questions. Omitting income overstates how cheap an asset looked and understates what an owner received.

Decision exercise: buy A$20, receive A$0.80, sell A$19.60, costs A$0.10. Price return = -2.0%. Total return before costs = (-0.40 + 0.80) / 20 = +2.0%. Net total return = (0.40 - 0.10) / 20 = +1.5%. Report the net figure.

Common errors: mixing a price index with a total-return portfolio; forgetting special dividends; and using trade currency when your account is reported in another currency.
tts.m03.l2:
Why it matters: compounding is why a string of moderate gains or losses is not the same as adding the percentages.

Decision exercise: three months of +5%, -3% and +4%. Cumulative = 1.05 x 0.97 x 1.04 - 1 = 5.9%, not 6%. Annualising that 5.9% as if it were a sustainable yearly rate would be dishonest.

Never annualise a few days of results. A 2% week is not evidence of a 180% year.
tts.m03.l3:
Why it matters: drawdown is the path a human (or an AI risk rule) actually has to live through.

Recovery arithmetic is unforgiving: a 30% loss needs about 42.9% to recover (1/0.70 - 1). That is why risk caps exist. It is also why no published recovery percentage is a promise you will get the required gain.

Common error: quoting average return without the worst peak-to-trough decline in the same window.
tts.m03.l4:
Why it matters: picking only closed winners is the simplest way to fake skill.

Decision exercise: list realised P&L, unrealised P&L and itemised costs for a fictional week, then refuse to quote any of those numbers alone as the headline.

Common errors: hiding financing on leveraged products; omitting FX conversion; and marking illiquid paper positions at last trade without noting uncertainty.
tts.m03.l5:
Why it matters: cashflows are not performance. TWR asks how the strategy did; IRR asks how your timing of deposits did. Honest reporting often needs both, labelled.

Decision exercise: start A$8,000, rise to A$8,800 (+10%), withdraw A$800, then fall to A$7,200. After the withdrawal the account was A$8,000, so the second period is 7,200/8,000 - 1 = -10%. TWR = 1.10 x 0.90 - 1 = -1.0%, even though the cash ending value is A$7,200 after a withdrawal.
tts.m03.l6: Use the seven-question template as a grading artefact: if any answer is missing, the statement is incomplete even if the return looks attractive. Paper versus live must be labelled every time.
tts.m04.l1:
Why it matters: policy rates change the discount rate and the cost of leverage throughout the financial system, but they do so with lags and with no guarantee about the next equity or FX move.

Decision exercise: read the latest decision page of one central bank (not a headline recap) and write: the target or range, the date, and one implementation detail the bank itself describes. For the RBA, that includes the cash-rate target and the corridor around Exchange Settlement balances described in this lesson.

Common errors: treating a 25 basis-point move as an immediate, one-for-one change in every mortgage or bond yield; and assuming every central bank uses the same corridor design.
tts.m04.l2:
Why it matters: if you cannot explain why price and yield move inversely, you will misread bond-fund headlines after rate news.

Worked check: the 2-year 5% coupon at a 4% yield was priced at about A$101.89 because the coupons are richer than the market now requires. If the yield rose to 5%, the same bond would be worth par. The mark-to-market loss is the cost of that yield rise even if coupons keep being paid.

Common errors: calling a government bond risk-free in real terms (inflation still matters); and confusing current yield with yield to maturity.
tts.m04.l3:
Why the sign must stay attached: dP/P is approximately minus modified duration times the yield change. If duration is 6 and yields fall 0.50%, the estimate is +3%, not -3%. Getting the sign wrong reverses every hedging decision.

Duration rises with maturity and falls as coupons increase, which is why a long zero has more interest-rate sensitivity than a short high-coupon note. Convexity means the straight-line duration estimate is imperfect for large moves; for ordinary (option-free) bonds, prices rise more and fall less than the line predicts.

Decision exercise: duration 4.5, yields rise 0.20%. Approximate price change = -4.5 x 0.20% = -0.90%.
tts.m04.l4:
Why it matters: the curve is a map of yields by maturity, not a crystal ball.

An inverted curve has preceded some recessions historically, but it is not a reliable timing tool and it is not a trade signal by itself. Steepening or flattening describes how the gap between two points changes.

Common error: treating one 2s10s observation as a complete macro view.
tts.m04.l5:
Why it matters: extra yield is compensation for something, usually default risk, uncertainty and lower liquidity. If the extra yield is smaller than a reasoned expected loss, it is not obviously generous.

Expected loss is approximately probability of default times loss given default. It is an estimate, not the actual loss that will occur.

Common errors: treating a rating as a guarantee; and ignoring that spreads can widen without any default if risk appetite falls.
tts.m04.l6: Re-check of the worked duration case: Macaulay duration 2.884 years and modified duration 2.747 were recomputed independently in this review from the listed cashflows and match the lesson. Use that habit: when a number matters, recompute it once from the cashflows rather than trusting a remembered figure.
tts.m05.l1:
Why it matters: every FX figure is a ratio. Reverse the base and the quote and you must invert the number, not subtract it from one.

Decision exercise: AUD/USD 0.7100. USD/AUD = 1 / 0.7100 = about 1.4085. If EUR/USD is 1.0850, EUR/AUD = 1.0850 / 0.7100 = about 1.5282. Write both results before you look at a calculator app's rounding.

The BIS April 2025 turnover figure (about US$9.6 trillion a day) is context for how large and continuous the market is, not a reason to use more leverage.
tts.m05.l2:
Why it matters: pip value depends on the pair's quoting convention and on the notional.

Worked check of the lesson example: buying 100,000 AUD costs 65,000 USD at 0.6500 and sells for 65,500 USD at 0.6550, a USD 500 profit. Converting that USD 500 into AUD at 0.6550 gives 500 / 0.6550 = about A$763. The conversion step uses the quote as USD per AUD, so you divide USD by the rate.

Common errors: treating every pip as 0.0001 (JPY pairs usually use 0.01); forgetting to convert P&L into home currency; and quoting pip P&L on the wrong notional.
tts.m05.l3:
Why it matters: a currency is a relative price of two economies' money. Many things move it, and none of them give a sure one-way bet.

Covered interest parity sets a no-arbitrage forward from spot and interest differentials. It is an accounting relationship for hedged interest, not a forecast that spot will travel to the forward. Trading as if the forward were a prediction is a category error.

Common errors: treating commodity-currency links as iron laws; and ignoring intervention or capital-flow surprises.
tts.m05.l4:
Why it matters: an unhedged foreign asset is always two trades, the asset and the currency.

Worked check: asset +8%, foreign currency +5% versus home: home-currency return = 1.08 x 1.05 - 1 = 13.4%. If instead the foreign currency falls 5%, the result is 1.08 x 0.95 - 1 = 2.6%. The sign on the FX leg matters as much as the asset leg.

Decision exercise: state whether your paper US-share position is intended to include USD exposure. If not, you need a hedge and you must account for its cost or benefit.
tts.m05.l5:
Why it matters: FX moves look small in pips and large once levered.

A carry trade earns a differential only while the high-yielder does not fall enough to erase it. Those falls often arrive quickly when risk appetite drops. Regulatory leverage caps on retail CFDs exist because unconstrained gearing turns ordinary moves into account-ending ones. This app remains paper-only.

Common error: choosing the maximum allowed leverage because it is allowed.
tts.m05.l6: Home-currency audit reminder: list each position's currency, whether it is hedged, and the approximate portfolio weight. Multiply unhedged weight by a plausible FX shock (the lesson used -8% on a 35% USD weight for a -2.8% portfolio hit) and ask whether that shock is inside your risk budget. If not, reduce weight or hedge in the paper plan.
tts.m06.l1:
Why it matters: calling something a commodity is not analysis. Oil, copper, wheat and gold respond to different inventories, weather, policy and financial conditions.

Decision exercise: pick one name from each group (energy, industrial metal, precious metal, agriculture) and write a single primary driver and one free official or exchange data source you could check. Do not invent a forecast.

Common error: treating a one-week inventory surprise as a complete thesis.
tts.m06.l2:
Why it matters: most people meet commodities through futures, not sacks of grain. The shape of the curve is part of the return.

If the front contract is A$80 and the next is A$76, the curve is in backwardation. A fund rolling from 80 down to 76, if prices otherwise stayed put, would book a positive roll of about 5% that month (buy the cheaper later contract). The opposite, rolling from 50 into 51, is about a 2% negative roll. These are illustrations, not predictions that spot will stay still.

Common errors: mixing calendar spreads with a view on the entire commodity complex; and forgetting contract specifications (units, delivery, tick value).
tts.m06.l3:
Why it matters: a flat spot price can still produce a large negative (or positive) fund return through roll and fees.

Worked reminder: 0.99^12 - 1 is about -11.4% from a 1% monthly negative roll, before adding collateral income and subtracting fees. Quote the compounding, not 12 times 1%.

If you cannot separate spot, roll, collateral and fees, you cannot explain a commodity ETF's year.
tts.m06.l4:
Why it matters: a producer equity is an operating business with costs, debt and hedges, not a clean units-of-commodity claim.

Operating leverage: cost A$70, price A$100, margin A$30. A 10% price rise to A$110 lifts margin by A$10, or about 33%. The same percentage price fall compresses the margin just as sharply.

Decision exercise: write whether your paper thesis is about the curve, the producer, or the exporter's currency. They are different bets.
tts.m06.l5:
Why it matters: free official series beat paid rumours for study.

The EIA weekly petroleum status report is one documented example (see the evidence register). Treat weekly data as revisable and seasonal. Read the latest release notes rather than a screenshot of one table.
tts.m06.l6: When comparing a futures fund with a producer, write two columns: what each wins if your price view is right, and what each can lose even if the price view is right (roll, hedge book, operational failure, currency). Neither column is a recommendation.
tts.m07.l1:
Why it matters: the label crypto covers very different claims, from a scarce network asset to a token that depends on a team's treasury.

Decision exercise: before any paper crypto position, write in one line what the token's holders actually have a claim on. If you cannot answer, size must be smaller, not larger.

Venue prices can differ. A print on one exchange is not automatically available on another.
tts.m07.l2:
Why it matters: operational loss (lost keys, insolvent custodian, irrecoverable transfer) can dominate market loss.

Moneysmart's warning that most crypto-assets are high-risk and that scams are common because transfers are hard to reverse is a reason for process, not a reason to hide the topic. New Australian digital-asset platform laws noted as commencing 8 April 2027 should be checked for their current status; this course does not give legal advice.

Decision exercise: list where the keys would live in your paper scenario and what failure that choice introduces.
tts.m07.l3:
Why it matters: higher volatility requires smaller notional for the same money risk.

Worked check: annualised volatility 70% and daily root using 365 gives about 3.7% for a one-standard-deviation day. That is a sizing input, not a promise that the next day will be that large or that small. Stress days can be several times larger.
tts.m07.l4:
Why it matters: perpetual swaps embed a running payment and a liquidation engine.

Worked check: +0.01% each 8 hours is 0.03% a day, about 11% a year if unchanged. High positive funding on a long is a cost that a backtest must include. At 20x, a 5% adverse move exhausts margin if there is no buffer: 1 / 20 = 5%.

Common error: treating funding as optional colour rather than P&L.
tts.m07.l5:
Why it matters: guaranteed-return language is a warning sign, not a feature.

Decision exercise: rewrite any marketing sentence that promises a fixed daily coin yield as a journal entry titled unverified claim, then refuse to size it until a primary source exists. There will not be one for a guaranteed 2% a day.
tts.m07.l6: The A$3,180 max-position example (A$400 risk, about 12.6% three-sigma daily move at 80% annualised volatility using 365) was recomputed independently in this review: 80 / sqrt(365) is about 4.19%, times 3 is about 12.56%, and 400 / 0.1256 is about A$3,185. Use the same method with your own volatility assumption and write the assumption down.
tts.m08.l1:
Why it matters: futures quantity is notional, not margin. Mixing them up explodes apparent returns and hides risk.

Worked quantity check: multiplier A$25 per index point and index 7,800 gives notional = 25 x 7,800 = A$195,000. A 1% index fall is 78 points and A$1,950. If initial margin is 6% (A$11,700), that 1% index move is about 17% of margin. The loss is A$1,950, not 1% of A$11,700.

A forward is customised and typically not exchange-margined in the same way; counterparty risk then sits with the other party rather than a central clearer.
tts.m08.l2:
Why it matters: payoff diagrams make the maximum loss and the breakeven visible before you argue about direction.

Call buyer breakeven = strike + premium. Put buyer breakeven = strike - premium. At expiry a long call on a share finishing below the strike loses the entire premium, not zero and not the strike.

Selling naked calls has theoretically unlimited loss. That is a sizing and permission issue, not a clever income idea.
tts.m08.l3:
Why it matters: Greeks are local, model-based sensitivities. They change as the market moves.

Delta 0.40 means about A$0.40 of option-price change for a A$1 underlying move, nearby, not forever. Gamma describes how quickly that delta changes. Theta is the cost of waiting for a long option. Vega is sensitivity to implied volatility, which can fall even when you are right on direction.

Common error: treating a morning delta as still true after a large move.
tts.m08.l4:
Share-margin worked case (US investor-education example, not an Australian rule and not a recommendation). The SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy's Investor Bulletin Understanding Margin Accounts (10 June 2021), read in full from investor.gov, states that under Regulation T you may borrow up to 50 percent of the purchase price of margin securities (initial margin), that some firms require more, and that FINRA rules require a maintenance requirement of at least 25 percent of the total market value of the margin securities, while many firms set higher house requirements, typically 30 to 40 percent or more. The bulletin's own example: you buy US$16,000 of securities by borrowing US$8,000 and paying US$8,000. If market value falls to US$12,000, equity is US$12,000 - US$8,000 = US$4,000. At a 25 percent maintenance requirement you need 0.25 x 12,000 = US$3,000, so US$4,000 still meets it. At a 40 percent house requirement you need 0.40 x 12,000 = US$4,800. Equity is then US$800 short, and the firm may issue a margin call for that US$800. The same bulletin warns that you can lose more than you invested; the firm may sell securities without notice and without letting you choose which names; it may raise house requirements without advance notice; and you are not entitled to an extension of time.

Australian retail CFD margins remain the separate ASIC PIO minima already taught in this lesson (3.33% major FX, 5% major index / minor FX / gold, 10% minor index and other commodities, 50% crypto, 20% other such as shares), with close-out and negative-balance protection, and with the order's dated consultation status. Do not import US share-margin percentages into an Australian CFD account, or the reverse.

Leverage identity: at 20:1, notional / margin = 20, so a 5% adverse move on notional equals 100% of margin. That identity is arithmetic, not a forecast.
tts.m08.l5:
Why it matters: a hedge is a second position with its own cost and basis risk, not an eraser.

Decision exercise: a protective put costing 3% of portfolio value per year caps downside below the strike and reduces returns by roughly that premium if markets rise. Write whether that cost is acceptable for the risk being reduced. If you cannot name the risk, it is not a hedge.
tts.m08.l6:
Greeks check: delta 0.52 + half gamma 0.03 + theta -0.04 = +0.51, matching the lesson's approximate next-day value of A$2.51 if the share rises A$1 with unchanged implied volatility. A five-point implied-vol fall at 0.08 vega per point, plus theta, is about -0.44 with the share unchanged. Direction can be right and the option still lose money.

Do not equate unused margin with unused risk.
tts.m09.l1:
Why it matters: liquidity is about the size you can transact near the current price, not about whether a quote exists.

Decision exercise: your order is 8% of ADV. Using the lesson's rule of thumb that 10% of ADV in one go often moves price, write whether you will split, use a limit, or skip. Then record displayed depth at the first two levels if you can see them.

Common error: treating yesterday's ADV as a guarantee of today's depth, especially around news.
tts.m09.l2:
Why it matters: slippage is often larger than brokerage and is invisible if you only record last price.

Worked check: decision mid A$5.00, fill A$5.03, 10,000 shares, slippage = A$300 or 0.60%. The square-root impact sketch (k times volatility times sqrt(size/ADV)) is a comparison tool, not a precise forecast.

Paper engines that fill at mid hide this cost. Add an assumption rather than pretend it is zero.
tts.m09.l3:
Why it matters: carry can turn a correct directional view into a net loss if you stay too long.

Worked check: A$20,000 short, 2% annual borrow, 30/365 days: 20,000 x 0.02 x 30/365 = about A$32.88, matching the lesson. Hard-to-borrow names can gap to much higher fees or be recalled.

FX conversion margins apply each way when you move between currencies.
tts.m09.l4: Tax remains general information only. The ATO CGT-discount description already in this lesson (including the foreign/temporary-resident exclusion, the 12-month rule excluding acquisition and CGT-event days, losses first, and the Budget 2026-27 caveat on the page dated 29 June 2026) should be re-checked on the official page before anyone relies on it. This course does not compute a learner's tax or give tax advice.
tts.m09.l5:
Why it matters: execution choice is part of expected return.

Prefer limits when you can wait; respect auctions if you intend to participate in them; avoid becoming a large fraction of a thin book. Measure paper fills against arrival mid so that improvement is visible.
tts.m09.l6: Implementation-shortfall check: average fill A$4.027 versus A$4.00 mid is 67.5 bps or A$540 on 20,000 shares, plus A$40 brokerage, about A$580 or 0.73%. If the idea only had 1% of expected edge, costs consumed most of it. That arithmetic is why mid-price backtests mislead.
tts.m10.l1:
Why it matters: margins tell you what is left after each layer of cost. Comparing companies without matching the layer (gross versus EBIT versus net) is a category error.

Worked check of the fictional figures: revenue 500, COGS 300, gross 200 (40%); after opex 120, EBIT 80 (16%); EBITDA 100 once D&A of 20 is added back; net 49 (9.8%). EBITDA is not cash and ignores capex.

Decision exercise: recompute each margin from a real annual report's numbers and write the page you took them from.
tts.m10.l2:
Why it matters: solvency and liquidity live on the balance sheet, not only in the earnings headline.

Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities. Net debt = borrowings minus cash (definitions vary slightly by company; read the note). A low current ratio with large near-term debt is a different risk than a high net-debt/EBITDA funded by long maturities.

Common error: treating book equity as what shareholders would receive in a sale tomorrow.
tts.m10.l3:
Why it matters: profit can rise while the business consumes cash.

Worked reminder: net profit 49, add D&A 20, subtract a A$15 receivables increase, approximate OCF 54; subtract capex 30, FCF 24. If receivables keep growing faster than sales, ask whether earnings quality is deteriorating.

FCF definitions also vary (leases, interest, acquisitions). Write the definition you used.
tts.m10.l4:
Why it matters: the three statements are one system. If they do not reconcile, you are missing a note or a classification.

Decision exercise: trace one year's net profit into retained earnings and one year's capex into the asset line, using a real report. If you cannot, you are not finished reading.
tts.m10.l5:
Why it matters: quality problems often show up first as unusual relationships, not as a single shocking number.

Receivables growing much faster than revenue, recurring one-off adjustments, and auditor changes are prompts to read notes, not automatic proof of fraud. Standards differ (IFRS/AASB versus US GAAP). Compare like with like.
tts.m10.l6: Receivable-days check: 110/520 x 365 is about 77 days; 180/600 x 365 is about 110 days. Profit up, operating cash flow down, days up: the right response is a list of questions, not an immediate valuation slogan.
tts.m11.l1:
Why it matters: a multiple is a price divided by a base. If the base is peak-cycle, unusual, or not comparable, the multiple is decorative.

P/E uses equity value and earnings. EV/EBITDA uses enterprise value and a pre-interest base, so it is better for comparing firms with different debt, provided you compute EV consistently (market cap plus net debt and other claims). P/B is more useful where book value is meaningful, such as many banks, and less useful where book ignores the main assets.

Decision exercise: using the fictional P/E of 12.5 (A$20 / A$1.60) and EV/EBITDA of 10x, write one reason each multiple could be misleading (for example, one-off earnings, or capex ignored by EBITDA).
tts.m11.l2:
Why it matters: yields look comparable only after you know whether income is cash, franked, or a one-off.

The franking example in this lesson uses a 30% illustrative company tax rate for imputation and notes that base-rate entities may use 25% from 2021-22 per the ATO page dated 9 December 2020. Check the current official page and the paying entity before using either rate. Grossed-up yield = cash yield / (1 - company tax rate used for franking) when the dividend is fully franked.

FCF yield = FCF / market cap (or sometimes equity FCF definitions). Write the FCF definition.
tts.m11.l3:
Why it matters: discounted cash flow turns assumptions into a number that looks more precise than it is.

Gordon terminal value = next FCF / (r - g) is undefined or explosive if g is close to r, and it is nonsense if g exceeds a reasoned long-run nominal growth rate for the economy. Sensitivity is the point of the exercise: the lesson's shift from r = 9% to r = 8% moved terminal value from A$166.7m to A$200m on the same A$10m FCF.

Decision exercise: refuse to publish a single point value. Publish a range and the assumptions that drive it.
tts.m11.l4:
Why it matters: unit metrics translate a business model into numbers you can compare, but companies define many of them differently.

Subscription LTV using ARPU x gross margin / monthly churn assumes a constant churn and margin forever. In the lesson, 30 x 0.70 / 0.02 = A$1,050. If monthly churn is actually 3%, LTV falls to A$700 and LTV/CAC at a A$350 CAC drops from 3.0 to 2.0. Always read the company's definition of ARPU, churn and CAC.

Other unit metrics taught later by sector (AISC, RASK/CASK, NIM, combined ratio, cap rate) have the same rule: write the definition before you compare two firms.
tts.m11.l5:
Why it matters: cheapness without a reason is often a warning.

Peak-cycle earnings, one-off gains, upcoming dilution and unsustainable dividends are standard traps. Compare with history and with peers, then check whether earnings turn into cash.
tts.m11.l6: The scenario grid (A$4.25 to A$9.11) is the product: a range plus uncertainty, not a buy call at A$6.00. If an AI tool outputs a single fair value without the grid, ask it for the r and g assumptions and recompute.
tts.m12.l1:
Why it matters: a bank's earnings are a spread business with a credit overlay.

NIM = net interest income / average interest-earning assets. The fictional 18 / 900 = 2.0% is a level, not a quality score, until you know mix (mortgages versus unsecured), hedging and how quickly deposits reprice. Cost-to-income shows efficiency; loan-loss rates show credit cost.

Decision exercise: if NIM widens 10 basis points on A$900bn of earning assets, that is about A$0.9bn of extra NII before losses. Ask what extra impairments might arrive later in the same rate cycle.
tts.m12.l2:
Why it matters: capital and funding are what keep a bank open when loans sour or deposits leave.

CET1 ratio = common equity tier 1 / risk-weighted assets is general Basel-style terminology used in this course as a reference. This review did not newly verify a specific APRA numerical minimum from primary text, so treat any number you see in a bank report as that bank's reported figure against its regulator's current rules, not as a universal legal minimum taught here. LCR and NSFR are likewise general names for liquidity and stable-funding metrics; read the regulator and the bank's disclosure rather than memorising an unverified threshold.

High ROE produced by thin capital is a risk statement, not a compliment.
tts.m12.l3:
Why it matters: bank earnings are cyclical even when they look dull.

Credit growth, underwriting standards, house prices and unemployment tend to move together over a cycle. Rising rates can lift NIM first and lift defaults later. Watch arrears and published stress tests as process checks, not as guarantees of future losses.

Decision exercise: write one leading indicator you will record for a paper bank position (for example, 90-day arrears) and the change that would make you review the thesis.
tts.m12.l4:
Why it matters: an insurer can look profitable until reserves prove thin or a catastrophe arrives.

Combined ratio = (claims + expenses) / net earned premium. Below 100% is an underwriting profit; above 100% is an underwriting loss. The fictional 93% (650 + 280) / 1,000 leaves investment income on float as additional, separate earnings. Life insurers add rate and longevity sensitivity.

Common error: treating last year's combined ratio as the expected cost of next year's catastrophe.
tts.m12.l5:
Why it matters: market-infrastructure and asset-management revenues often scale with activity or with asset prices.

Worked check: AUM A$100bn at 0.40% is A$400m of revenue. A 15% market fall with no flows leaves A$85bn and A$340m. Outflows make that worse. Exchange and payments volumes can rise in volatile years even as asset managers suffer.

These are GICS Financials business models alongside banks and insurers; do not analyse them as if they were loan books.
tts.m12.l6: Stress arithmetic check: extra impairments of 0.48% on A$600bn of loans equal A$2.88bn. Against A$12bn of pre-provision profit that is about 24% of that profit before tax. The lesson no longer claims capital is far above minima; it says that if capital remains above the relevant regulator's requirements the dividend may be maintained, but that is not certain. That wording should stay cautious.
tts.m13.l1:
Energy (GICS Energy) metric interpretation. Upstream cash margin is roughly realised price minus lifting cost and royalties; reserve life = reserves / annual production; breakeven is the price at which a project or firm covers the cost definition the company is using (those definitions vary). Midstream fee-based tariffs are less directly tied to the commodity price. Downstream crack spread is refined-product value minus crude cost.

Worked reminder: reserve life 200m boe / 20m boe per year = 10 years. That is a ratio, not a promise the field produces evenly for a decade.

Spot-price valuation trap: multiplying last week's oil price by current production as if it were a perpetual annuity ignores decline, reinvestment and the cycle.
tts.m13.l2:
Materials / mining metric interpretation. Grade (g/t or %) drives how much metal you get from a tonne of ore. AISC and C1 are cost metrics whose company definitions are not identical; read the reconciliation. JORC Ore Reserves are the economically mineable part of Measured and/or Indicated Mineral Resources, including dilution and losses, supported by pre-feasibility or feasibility studies (JORC Code 2012, as already cited). Resources are not automatically mineable. Other jurisdictions use other codes; this course does not treat SEC S-K 1300 as a verified parallel definition.

Worked reminder: gold A$3,200, AISC A$2,400, 250 koz gives (800 x 250,000) = A$200m of all-in margin before other corporate items.
tts.m13.l3: Utilities metric interpretation. Allowed return on a regulated asset base is a building block of allowed revenue, not a guaranteed shareholder return after gearing, opex overruns and regulatory resets. Example: RAB A$8bn times 5.5% = A$440m return component. Higher bond yields often pressure valuations because those cashflows are compared with bonds. Unregulated generation is a different, more commodity-like risk.
tts.m13.l4: Transition and policy risks can change asset lives and required capex. Treat them as scenarios (carbon price, demand shift, permitting delay), not as a single ESG score. Critical-mineral prices can boom and bust as supply responds; that is cycle behaviour again.
tts.m13.l5:
Why mid-cycle thinking exists: energy and mining earnings swing with commodity prices and with operating leverage. Using spot peaks as the base for a multiple is how expensive assets look cheap. Write the commodity price you used in any valuation sentence.

Shares often move before the commodity as investors anticipate the next part of the cycle; that lead-lag is a tendency, not a timing system.
tts.m13.l6: Cross-check of operating leverage: 50m boe at a A$60 cash margin (A$90 price minus A$30 cost) is A$3.0bn; at a A$30 margin (A$60 price) it is A$1.5bn. A one-third price fall halved the margin because costs are sticky. Use that pattern when you stress a producer, a miner, or (less directly) a commodity-linked utility input.
tts.m14.l1:
Information Technology / software metric interpretation. ARR is a company-defined run-rate of recurring revenue, not an IFRS line you can assume is comparable. NRR above 100% means existing customers spent more (up-sell net of churn); below 100% means the base shrank. Rule of 40 (growth % plus a profit-margin %) is a heuristic, not a law: 30% growth and 5% FCF margin scores 35. Stock-based compensation is a real economic cost because it dilutes owners.

Decision exercise: recompute FCF after subtracting SBC and see whether the quality story changes, as in the later deep-dive case.
tts.m14.l2:
Semiconductors and AI-infrastructure metric interpretation. Book-to-bill below 1 means new orders are running behind current billings, often an early-cycle warning. Inventory days rising while book-to-bill falls is a classic correction signal, not a proof of disaster. Customer concentration (a few cloud buyers of AI chips, for example) is a risk metric as much as a growth story.

Capex guidance from large purchasers can move an entire supplier set. Treat it as demand colour, and remember guidance changes.
tts.m14.l3:
Communication Services metric interpretation. Telecoms: ARPU, churn, subscribers, capex/revenue and leverage. High capex intensity is normal for networks; FCF after spectrum outlays can look very different from EBITDA. Platforms: users, engagement and ad revenue per user. User growth without monetisation is not revenue.

Worked reminder: 10 million subscribers at A$50 a month is A$6bn a year. Monthly churn of 2% compounds to about 1 - 0.98^12 = 21.5% of the starting base over a year if there are no adds (the lesson's similar example used 1%).
tts.m14.l4:
Why it matters: narrative-heavy sectors reward people who separate booked revenue from plans.

Ask who pays today, at what margin, with what capex and with what competition. Apply the same scepticism to AI trading tools: fluency is not verification. A claim without a primary source stays in the unverified column.
tts.m14.l5: Platform and regulatory risks (antitrust, privacy, content rules, export controls, cyber incidents) can change a multiple faster than a quarterly KPI. Write them as scenario risks with a size implication (reduce, hedge, or avoid) rather than as footnotes you ignore until they hit the headline.
tts.m14.l6: SBC adjustment check: FCF A$250m minus SBC A$180m leaves A$70m, a 7% margin rather than 25%, on A$1bn of revenue. If you use the unadjusted figure to claim quality, you are choosing a definition that hides dilution. State the choice.
tts.m15.l1: Industrials metric interpretation. Backlog coverage = backlog / annual revenue; book-to-bill above 1 usually means the backlog is growing. Fixed-price contracts transfer cost-overrun risk to the contractor: a 5% overrun on a A$1bn job is A$50m. Airlines: load factor, RASK (revenue per available seat-km) minus CASK (cost per available seat-km). A 0.4c negative gap means the airline loses that amount on every available seat-km before other items; fuel and FX can erase a thin positive gap.
tts.m15.l2:
Consumer Staples versus Consumer Discretionary metric interpretation. Staples: split growth into volume versus price/mix and watch gross margin; price-led growth can fade when consumers trade down to private label. Discretionary: same-store (like-for-like) sales = traffic x ticket; inventory turns; and sensitivity to consumer credit and confidence. One quarter is not a trend.

Worked reminder: revenue +6% = price +8% and volume -2% is price-led. Ask whether volume can keep falling without becoming a volume problem.
tts.m15.l3: Health Care metric interpretation. Pipelines should be listed by phase without inventing success-rate percentages this course has not sourced. Patent cliffs are scheduled revenue risks. Reimbursement (who pays, at what rate) can matter as much as science. Regulator roles taught here: TGA (Australia; ARTG listing; not the subsidy decision), FDA (US safety, efficacy and security of drugs, biologics and devices), and EMA scientific recommendations as a basis for EU centralised authorisation. Binary trial results can move prices violently; size as event risk, not as ordinary swing risk.
tts.m15.l4: Real Estate / REIT metric interpretation. Cap rate = NOI / value, so value = NOI / cap rate. If NOI is A$30m and the cap rate is 6%, value is A$500m. If cap rates rise from 5% to 6% on A$60m of NOI, value falls from A$1.2bn to A$1.0bn, about -16.7%. Gearing = net debt / total assets (common disclosure; check the REIT's definition). WALE is the weighted average lease expiry; a short WALE with falling occupancy is a different risk than a long WALE to strong tenants. Valuations can lag traded markets, so NTA is not a hard floor.
tts.m15.l5:
GICS coverage check. MSCI and S&P Dow Jones Indices describe GICS as 11 sectors, 25 industry groups, 74 industries and 163 sub-industries (methodology dated August 2024, evidence E17): Energy, Materials, Industrials, Consumer Discretionary, Consumer Staples, Health Care, Financials, Information Technology, Communication Services, Utilities and Real Estate. Sector-rotation stories (defensives in slowdowns, cyclicals in recoveries) are tendencies, not rules, and they do not replace unit-metric work.

If you cannot name a useful metric for each of those 11 sectors, return to Modules 12 to 15 before treating a rotation call as analysis.
tts.m15.l6: Integrated decision exercise: take one name from each remaining GICS sector you have not already used this week and write, in one line each, the metric, the number, the definition, and one limitation (company-defined metric, cyclical base, regulatory reset, binary event, or valuation lag). That list is the practical evidence for this module, not a profit target.
